transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in today?

Hi Dr. Smith. I'm here because... well, I just can't stop going back over the same spreadsheets and calculations at work again and again. I end up staying at the office for hours after everyone else leaves. Even when I know I already checked them, I just... I feel like I have to do it one more time. Because if I don't, I get this intense feeling that something bad is going to happen and it'll be my fault. It's just gotten really out of hand.

When you feel the urge to recheck the spreadsheets, is it because a specific unwanted thought or image keeps popping into your mind that you can't shake off, or is it more that you feel things simply have to be done in a particular exact way to feel right?

It's definitely a specific thought. Even after I check and I know the numbers match, this thought just keeps jumping into my head that I missed one hidden mistake somewhere in payroll or the taxes. I start thinking that somebody's check won't go through, or that the firm will get in trouble. I try to push it away, but... it just comes right back. It's like I can't trust my own eyes anymore.

latest_inference.note: The patient describes classic obsessions (intrusive, unwanted thoughts about hidden errors causing harm) coupled with compulsive checking behavior performed to reduce distress, despite recognizing the checking is excessive. This pattern is specific to OCD and argues against GAD (F41.1, which involves diffuse worry rather than discrete intrusive thoughts with ritualized compulsions), OCPD (F60.5, which reflects an ego-syntonic personality style of perfectionism rather than distressing intrusive thoughts), and depressive disorder (F32.1, no mood symptoms reported). This narrows the differential to OCD alone.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports recurrent, intrusive, unwanted thoughts (fear of hidden payroll/tax errors causing harm) that are recognized as excessive and distressing, followed by repetitive checking behaviors performed to reduce the anxiety these thoughts generate. The checking is time-consuming (hours after work), resistant to logical reassurance, and causes functional impairment (prolonged work hours, distress). This pattern of obsessions (intrusive thoughts) plus compulsions (repeated checking) performed to neutralize anxiety is characteristic of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (F42), rather than generalized anxiety (which lacks specific obsessive content) or obsessive-compulsive personality traits (which would involve pervasive rigidity/perfectionism without discrete intrusive thoughts).

confirmed_symptoms: Recurrent intrusive thought that a hidden error exists in payroll or tax calculations
Thought perceived as one's own but unwanted and hard to suppress
Attempts to resist or push away the thought are unsuccessful
Repeated rechecking of spreadsheets and calculations
Checking behavior performed to prevent feared negative outcome (checks not going through, firm getting in trouble)
Behavior is repetitive and not proportionate to actual risk
